findings.problem: orientation[3] states that 'A pharmacy that is not located in a high overdose area carries no continuous-supply duty under 247 CMR 9.06(2)', and role_duties[8] confines the continuous-supply, over-the-counter inclusion and notice duties to a pharmacy located in a high overdose area. The section never tells the candidate that the Board, which defines those areas (247 CMR 9.06(1)(a)) and determines them in consultation with the Department (s. 19C), has determined that every area of Massachusetts qualifies. It therefore teaches as live a distinction between pharmacies inside and outside such areas that has no current Massachusetts application.
findings.rationale: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2024-01 (adopted 1/11/24, revised 2/6/25), which the current pharmacist naloxone standing order cites, states that because all areas of Massachusetts experience high incidences of opioid-related overdoses or deaths, 'Massachusetts pharmacies are required to stock naloxone in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, § 19C', and that pharmacies must maintain a continuous, sufficient supply. Item 60 of the Board's Retail Compliance Inspection Report checks retail pharmacies against that statement, citing 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) and (b) and the policy. The regulatory text is quoted accurately, but a candidate applying the section to a Massachusetts pharmacy in a low-overdose town would conclude that it need not keep naloxone in stock, contrary to the Board's position; on the same determination the s. 19C over-the-counter and notice provisos also reach every Massachusetts pharmacy. The fix is to state the Board's statewide determination and qualify the location-based statements.

findings.problem: exceptions[2] teaches, as an exception to the continuous-supply duty, that 'a pharmacy elsewhere' (outside a high overdose area) may dispense under the statewide standing order or a prescription on complying with the rest of 247 CMR 9.06, without the continuous-supply duty. It omits that the Board has determined that all areas of Massachusetts are high-incidence areas, so the carve-out currently reaches no Massachusetts pharmacy.
findings.rationale: 247 CMR 9.06(1)(a) makes the category depend on the Board's published determination, and Board Policy 2024-01 and the Board's retail inspection form apply the stocking requirement to Massachusetts pharmacies generally, the form citing 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) and (b) together. An exception that is textually accurate but not operative on Massachusetts facts, taught as operative, invites a wrong answer to whether a particular Massachusetts pharmacy may go without naloxone stock. It shares its root cause with the actor_and_scope finding; one edit resolves both.

findings.problem: The study aids tell the candidate to test whether the pharmacy is on the Board's list before applying the continuous-supply duty and the s. 19C notice: decision_logic[6] opens its second limb with 'If the pharmacy is located in a high overdose area', comparison_tables[1].rows[4] gives the trigger as location in an area on the list the Board publishes, and forms_records[4] says a pharmacy's location in a listed area is what brings the duty. None of them records that the Board has treated the whole Commonwealth as qualifying.
findings.rationale: Because Board Policy 2024-01 and the Board's inspection form apply the requirement statewide, these decision aids would lead a candidate to look for a municipality list and to treat an unlisted pharmacy as outside the duty. The aids are otherwise accurate paraphrases of 247 CMR 9.06(1)(a) and (2)(a). This is the same root cause as the actor_and_scope and material_exceptions findings, recorded here for the aids a candidate would actually apply to facts.

findings.problem: The section teaches the s. 19B(d) duty as an annual report by the dispensing pharmacist, which is accurate to the statute, but does not mention how the Board has implemented that report. worked_examples[2].steps[5] also answers a compliance note in which 'the pharmacy' sends the report by telling the reader to keep the actor straight, which could be read as saying a pharmacy-level report names the wrong actor.
findings.rationale: Board Policy 2024-01, section II, has the pharmacy report naloxone doses: preferably through its daily Prescription Monitoring Program submissions (for data collection only, not shown on a patient's PMP profile), and otherwise by an emailed annual report due by January 15 giving the pharmacy's name and zip code, the total naloxone doses dispensed and the number paid for with insurance; section I.E of the same policy has 'Naloxone Rescue Kit' used in place of the purchaser's name and address, consistent with the statutory bar on identifying patients. The section's declared scope is the statutory reporting provisions and its statements are correct, so this is Low; adding the Board's January 15 date, the PMP route and the pharmacy's role would prevent confusion on Massachusetts facts.

authorities.exact_section: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2024-01: Naloxone Dispensing (adopted 1/11/24, revised 2/6/25), introduction and sections I-III

findings.problem: The section recommends, as 'the course that is safe on either reading', that a pharmacy provide counseling and the opioid antagonist information pamphlet whenever it hands over any opioid antagonist, over-the-counter packages included. That recommendation is the author's own, rests on no cited authority, and sits uneasily with official guidance on over-the-counter naloxone.
findings.rationale: It is true that universal counseling cannot breach 247 CMR 9.06(3), and the section correctly says the provisions do not address over-the-counter packages in terms. But DPH's memorandum on OTC naloxone (12/20/2023) asks retailers to enable anonymous access directly on a shelf without contacting an employee, the DCP advisory (10/10/2024) says the Drug Control Program's regulations do not apply to OTC naloxone, and Board Policy 2024-01 places its counseling-and-pamphlet instruction within dispensing by patient-specific prescription or the standing order and says nothing about OTC sales. Presented as the legally safe course, the recommendation could lead a candidate to treat counseling and a pamphlet as expected on an ordinary OTC sale. Low, because it is expressly hedged and asserts no mandate.

results.summary: Verified on 2026-09-14 against the current official texts: M.G.L. c. 94C ss. 19(d), 19A, 19B, 19C and 19E (and the s. 18D, s. 21, s. 19F and s. 34A pointers) on malegislature.gov; 247 CMR 9.06 (PDF dated 12/6/24); the current 39-page 105 CMR 700.000 for 700.003(F), 700.004(B)(7) and (B)(11); the DCP advisory of 10/10/2024; and, for Massachusetts practice, Board Policy 2024-01, the current pharmacist naloxone standing order, DPH's emergency contraception pharmacy guidance and the Board's retail inspection form. Quotations and paraphrases are faithful throughout. The section correctly separates the three standing-order regimes by definition, issuer and modality (s. 19A(b) shall; s. 19B(b) and s. 19E(b) may), training (permissive for emergency contraception, mandatory only before dispensing a COVID-19 drug, none in s. 19B or 247 CMR 9.06, which the pharmacist naloxone standing order and DPH's emergency contraception guidance bear out) and reporting (annual, annual, upon request; the no-identification sentence absent from s. 19E(d); confidentiality and public-records exclusion in all three; no aggregate report in s. 19A). It confines the s. 19B(e) purchaser-billing rule to dispensing pursuant to s. 19B, and states the over-the-counter and prescription naloxone distinction, the (B)(11) and (B)(7) exemptions and the two-instrument gate in 105 CMR 700.003(F) accurately. All seven practice questions are answerable from the section and none is contradicted. One defect: the section presents the 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) continuous-supply duty and the s. 19C provisos as reaching only pharmacies in listed high overdose areas and says a pharmacy outside such an area has no continuous-supply duty, omitting the Board's determination in Policy 2024-01 that all areas of Massachusetts qualify and that Massachusetts pharmacies must stock naloxone continuously; this is recorded as three Medium findings sharing one root cause (scope, exception, study aids). Two Low observations concern the Board's reporting mechanics and an unsupported 'safe course' recommendation for over-the-counter hand-overs. The COVID-19 standing-order PDFs on mass.gov are image-only and were not relied on. MINOR_EDIT: a short addition stating the Board's statewide determination, with the location-based statements qualified, would make the section publishable.
